source.title: Select, Hypothesize and Verify: Towards Verified Neuron Concept Interpretation
source.authors: Ze-Bin Ji; Yang Hu; Xiu-Li Bi; Bo Liu; Bin Xiao

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses whether neurons have well-defined functions and presents its own neuron-interpretation results, but it does not measure the prevalence of polysemantic neurons or test whether their mixed responses are unrelated. Its reported neuron-ablation example concerns a different question: whether a particular proposed concept aligns with class-specific model behavior.
record.gate_note: The paper proposes SIEVE, which selects high-activation samples, generates neuron-concept hypotheses, and checks them using activation rates on generated images. Its mean Activation Rate comparisons evaluate the interpretation method, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how common that is, or whether mixed responses share a feature. The text also reports a neuron-ablation example (Neuron 39 responds to cat eyes and ablation predominantly degrades feline-category accuracy); this is recorded as a related finding, not evidence for or against the listed versions. No results quantify polysemantic-neuron prevalence.
record.test_reason: SIEVE is a neuron-concept interpretation method for vision classifiers. Its results (mean Activation Rate vs baselines, ablations, threshold sweep, domain shift) evaluate the method, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs or how often. The clustering step yields multiple concepts per neuron (e.g. ViT neuron 361 gets two descriptions), but the paper never quantifies or classifies these as polysemantic or unrelated. The neuron 39 ablation concerns one concept's alignment with class accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance: authors argue existing methods wrongly assume every neuron captures discriminative features and every generated concept is accurate; SIEVE filters low-discrimination neurons and verifies concepts, giving ~1.5x higher mean Activation Rate than the best baseline.
record.recipe_differences: SIEVE is a neuron-concept interpretation and verification framework, not a reproduction of a method for measuring polysemanticity. It selects samples, clusters activation patterns, hypothesizes concepts, and verifies them using generated images and activation rates.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that changing the activation threshold β has minimal impact on its interpretation metrics. This is not a test of sensitivity in polysemantic-neuron measurement.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating ResNet-50 neuron 39 (described as cat eyes) mainly lowers accuracy on feline classes; similar pattern reported in ViT-B/16.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some penultimate-layer vision neurons have concept-specific causal effects on related classes.

fits_no_version.finding: Paper distinguishes high-discrimination neurons (consistent high-activation patterns) from low-discrimination neurons with scattered responses, using 99th-percentile/median ratio; no prevalence reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some vision neurons lack a clear activation preference (low-discrimination), distinct from polysemanticity.

record.problems: The ablation example is reported qualitatively in the text, with its plotted values only in a figure; no uncertainty estimates or control result are stated for that example. The paper does not quantify the prevalence of polysemantic neurons.
record.rows_left_out: No mean Activation Rate benchmark, threshold sweep, ablation-table, or domain-shift rows were included: those results evaluate SIEVE or neuron-concept interpretation metrics, not polysemanticity or any listed version.

untested.parts: Does not report whether or how often penultimate-layer neurons in ResNet/ViT respond to unrelated inputs; multi-concept clusters are shown qualitatively only, without relatedness judgments.
No test of initialization, regularization or noise as causes.
No comparison of polysemantic share across architectures or activation functions.
Does not examine canonical polysemantic neurons for shared features.
Threshold β and Top-1% activation threshold change interpretation metrics only (minimal effect), not polysemanticity classification.

record.verdict_notes: Record's relation/tranche (discusses/T6) and empty labels are appropriate. Multi-concept descriptions per neuron are a method feature, not evidence on polysemanticity's prevalence or unrelatedness.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether vision-model neurons respond to several unrelated inputs.
No language models or transformer MLP neuron polysemanticity are tested.
Does not test superposition or capacity pressure as the cause of polysemanticity.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
Does not compare architectures or activation functions for their effect on the share of polysemantic neurons, or measure a performance tradeoff from reducing that share.
Does not investigate canonical polysemantic neurons to determine whether their mixed inputs share a feature or are related jobs.

Although the paper varies sample-selection thresholds and uses an activation threshold for its metric, it does not measure how those choices change the classification or prevalence of polysemantic neurons.

rows.note: The text describes a targeted class-specific accuracy drop, but numerical values are shown only in the figure. This is evidence about one proposed neuron function, not a test of polysemanticity.
rows.check: Single-neuron ablation showing concept-aligned class accuracy drop; not a measure of polysemanticity. 'observed' only refers to the paper's own claim about this neuron, values are figure-only.

relation.reason: No version is tested. The paper mentions only in passing that clustering reveals 'multiple potential functions a single neuron may correspond to'. Borderline with 'assumes', since the clustering step presumes multi-pattern neurons, but the clusters are not shown to be unrelated concepts.

tranche.reason: SIEVE is a neuron-concept interpretation and verification method. Its results (mean AR vs baselines, ablation, beta sweep, domain shift) evaluate the method. It reports no measure of how often neurons respond to unrelated inputs, and the term polysemantic never appears.

source_check.notes: Both rows are single-neuron ablation illustrations (one is figure-only, the other is vague), so they are not polysemanticity evidence. The multi-concept examples (Fig. 1 ResNet-18 neuron 162 with two hypothesized concepts, one failing verification at AR 0.26 vs 0.98; Fig. 4 ViT-B/16 neuron 361 with two descriptions) are anecdotes not framed as polysemanticity, and they involve related, not unrelated, concepts. No verdicts are warranted.
